# Vascular physiology

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Basics of cardiology > Vascular physiology*

[Original Article Link](/library/jJ0_FS)

---

## Summary

The <u>circulatory system</u>, which is also called the vascular system or <u>cardiovascular system</u>, consists of the <u>systemic circulation</u>, <u>pulmonary circulation</u>, the <u>heart</u>, and <u>the lymphatic system</u>. Blood flow through the <u>circulatory system</u> is generated by the <u>heart</u>. <u>Vascular resistance</u> is the amount of resistance in the systematic circulation that must be overcome to create blood flow. The <u>Poiseuille equation</u> describes the relationship between <u>vascular resistance</u>, the length and radius of the vessel, and the viscosity of blood. Blood pressure is generated by the <u>heart</u>, creating a pulsatile blood flow that leads to systolic blood pressure (maximum pressure reached during a <u>cardiac cycle</u>) and <u>diastolic</u> blood pressure (minimum pressure reached during a <u>cardiac cycle</u>) within the <u>circulatory system</u>. The pressure gradient across the <u>circulatory system</u> drives the blood flow from high pressure to low pressure. <u>Blood pressure regulation</u> involves a complex interaction of various sensors (<u>baroreceptors</u>, <u>volume receptors</u>, <u>chemoreceptors</u>) and mechanisms, including the <u>autonomic nervous system</u>, the <u>renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system</u> (<u>RAAS</u>), and <u>atrial reflex</u> and <u>diuresis reflex</u>. <u>Perfusion</u> is the passage of the blood through the <u>circulatory system</u> to the <u>capillary bed</u> to deliver oxygen and <u>nutrients</u> to the tissue and remove waste products (e.g., removal of CO<sub>2</sub> to the <u>lungs</u>, removal of <u>urea</u> to the <u>kidneys</u>). <u>Perfusion</u> levels differ in organs and fluctuate depending on the activity (e.g., rest, physical activity). Autoregulatory mechanisms (<u>myogenic autoregulation</u>, local metabolite production), as well as central regulatory mechanisms, modulate <u>perfusion</u> levels in organs. The exchange of substances in the <u>microcirculation</u> occurs via <u>diffusion</u>, filtration, and reabsorption. <u>Capillary fluid exchange</u> is described by the <u>Starling equation</u>, which states that the net fluid flow is dependent on the <u>capillary</u> and <u>interstitial</u> hydrostatic pressures, oncotic pressures, and the vascular permeability to fluid and <u>proteins</u>.




The <u>heart</u> and <u>cardiac physiology</u>, as well as <u>the lymphatic system</u>, are discussed in separate articles.

---

## Circulatory system

* Systemic circulation

* Oxygenated blood flows from the left <u>heart</u> into the <u>systemic circulation</u> and, after passing through the <u>capillary bed</u>, flows back in a deoxygenated state to the <u>right atrium</u> of the <u>heart</u> to restart the process.

* Left <u>atrium</u> → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta→ <u>arteries</u> → <u>arterioles</u> → <u>capillary</u> beds → <u>veins</u> → <u>superior vena cava</u> (<u>SVC</u>) and <u>inferior vena cava</u> (<u>IVC</u>) → <u>right atrium</u>

* Pulmonary circulation

* Deoxygenated blood in the right <u>heart</u> flows into the <u>lungs</u>, where it is oxygenated and returned to the <u>left atrium</u>.

* Right <u>atrium</u> → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary trunk → <u>pulmonary arteries</u>  → <u>lungs</u>  → four <u>pulmonary veins</u>  → <u>left atrium</u>

* <u>Heart</u>: connects <u>systemic circulation</u> and <u>pulmonary circulation</u> (see “<u>Heart</u>” and “<u>Cardiac physiology</u>”)

* <u>Lymphatic system</u>: a network of lymphatic vessels that transport <u>lymph</u> toward the <u>heart</u> (see <u>lymphatic drainage</u> for details)

---

## Hemodynamics

### Pressure, flow, and resistance




The relationship between pressure, flow, and resistance in the <u>circulatory system</u> is expressed as ΔP = Q x R




* ΔP = pressure gradient

* Q = blood flow

* R = <u>vascular resistance</u>





### Blood flow




* Blood flow is driven by cardiac activity pumping blood through the <u>circulatory system</u>.

* Volume of blood the <u>heart</u> pumps through the <u>circulatory system</u> per minute = <u>cardiac output</u> (CO)

* Rate of blood flow = blood flow / total cross-sectional area of the blood vessel





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>capillaries</u> have the largest total cross-sectional area of all <u>blood vessels</u> (4,500–6,000 cm<sup>2</sup>) and, therefore, have the slowest body <u>velocity</u> (0.03 cm/s). The aorta, on the other hand, has the smallest cross-sectional area (3–5 cm<sup>2</sup>) but the highest blood <u>velocity</u> (40 cm/s).




#### Laminar and <u>turbulent blood flow</u>




Blood flow in vessels is either laminar or <u>turbulent</u> depending on the smoothness of the blood vessel walls, the viscosity of the blood, the blood <u>velocity</u>, and the diameter of the lumen.




* Laminar blood flow 

* Definition: a layered flow pattern

* Effect: The layer with the highest <u>velocity</u> flows in the center of the vessel lumen.

* <u>Reynolds number</u>: low

* Occurrence: throughout the vascular system

* Turbulent blood flow 

* Definition: a chaotic flow pattern

* Effects

* Increases <u>vascular resistance</u>

* Promotes <u>thrombus formation</u>

* Creates <u>murmurs</u> (e.g., <u>bruits</u> in a stenotic vessel)

* <u>Reynolds number</u>: high

* Occurrence

* Vessels with a large diameter (e.g., aorta)

* High viscosity

* Low viscosity (e.g., <u>anemia</u>)

* Vascular bifurcations

* Vascular stenosis

### Vascular resistance




* Definition: resistance in the <u>circulatory system</u> that must be overcome to create blood flow (R = ΔP / Q)

* Types of resistance

* Total peripheral resistance (TPR): the amount of resistance to blood flow in the systemic circulation = (<u>MAP</u> - <u>CVP</u>) / CO 

* ↑ TPR in <u>vasoconstriction</u> of <u>arterioles</u> (e.g., in hemorrhage, ↑ <u>vasopressor</u>) → ↑ <u>afterload</u> and ↓ <u>venous return</u> → ↓ CO

* ↓ TPR in vasodilation of <u>arterioles</u> (e.g., in exercise, AV shunts) → ↓ <u>afterload</u> and ↑ <u>venous return</u> → ↑ CO

* <u>Pulmonary vascular resistance</u>










#### Poiseuille equation




* This equation describes the relationship between <u>systemic vascular resistance</u> (R) and the length of the vessel (L), the radius of the vessel (r), and the viscosity of blood (η).

* Resistance to flow: R = 8ηL/(πr<sup>4</sup>)

* <u>Systemic vascular resistance</u> is inversely proportional to vessel radius to the 4<sup>th</sup> power.

* ↓ Vessel radius (i.e., <u>vasoconstriction</u>) → ↑ systemic vascular resistance → ↓ blood flow → ↑ pressure upstream (i.e., <u>MAP</u>) and ↓ pressure downstream (i.e., in <u>capillaries</u>)

* ↑ Vessel radius (i.e., <u>vasodilation</u>) → ↓ systemic vascular resistance → ↑ blood flow → ↓ <u>MAP</u> and ↑ <u>capillary</u> pressure

* <u>Systemic vascular resistance</u> is proportional to blood viscosity, which is primarily determined by <u>hematocrit</u>.

* ↑ Viscosity (e.g., <u>polycythemia</u>, hyperproteinemia) → ↑ <u>systemic vascular resistance</u>

* ↓ Viscosity (e.g., <u>anemia</u>) → ↓ resistance

* <u>Systemic vascular resistance</u> is proportional to blood vessel length.





> [!NOTE]
> Vascular stenosis (e.g., <u>coronary artery disease</u>) increases <u>systemic vascular resistance</u> significantly! When the length of the vessel and viscosity of the blood remain constant, the relationship between <u>systemic vascular resistance</u> and the radius of the vessel can be simplified to R ∼ 1/r<sup>4</sup>. So, if there is a 50% reduction in radius, R = 1/(0.5 x r)^4 → 1/(0.0625 x r<sup>4</sup>) → 16/r<sup>4</sup>, there is a 16x increase in resistance (1600%).

#### Serial and parallel circuits




The total resistance in <u>blood vessels</u> depends on whether these vessels are arranged as serial or parallel circuits.




|  | Serial circuit | Parallel circuit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | <br><br>* Total resistance is the sum of individual resistors (R<sub>x</sub> = <u>R<sub>1</sub></u> + <u>R<sub>2</sub></u> + R<sub>3</sub> … + R<sub>N</sub>).<br><br>* Total resistance is greater than individual resistors.<br><br>* Blood flow is the same in each vessel in a series circuit.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Total resistance is the sum of reciprocals of individual resistors (1/R<sub>x</sub> = 1/<u>R<sub>1</sub></u> + 1/<u>R<sub>2</sub></u> + 1/R<sub>3</sub>… + 1/R<sub>N</sub>) .<br><br>* Total resistance can be smaller than individual resistors.<br><br>* Pressure is the same in each vessel in a parallel network.<br><br><br> |
| Examples | <br>* An <u>artery</u> gives rise to two or more branches in series (e.g., <u>artery</u> branches into <u>arterioles</u>).<br><br> | <br>* An <u>artery</u> gives rise to two or more branches parallel to each other (e.g., <u>capillaries</u> in a <u>capillary bed</u>).<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Arterioles</u> are the <u>blood vessels</u> that contribute most to TPR and, therefore, also to <u>blood pressure regulation</u>.




![Resistance of vessels in series and in parallel](media/jimm70o6cihdd8zkbrrxts4r.jpg)

Resistance of vessels in series and in parallel




### Pressure




* Blood pressure is generated by the pumping of the <u>heart</u>, which results in pulsatile blood flow (ΔP = Q x R).
* The ΔP drives blood flow from high pressure to low pressure.

* Systolic blood pressure: maximum pressure reached during a <u>cardiac cycle</u>

* <u>Diastolic</u> blood pressure: minimum pressure reached during a <u>cardiac cycle</u>

* <u>Mean arterial pressure</u> (<u>MAP</u>): simplified value of systolic and <u>diastolic</u> blood pressure at <u>resting heart rate</u>

* <u>MAP</u> = ⅓ systolic pressure + ⅔ <u>diastolic</u> pressure

* <u>MAP</u> = CO × TPR

* Pulse pressure: the difference between <u>diastolic</u> blood pressure (DP) and systolic blood pressure (SP) of the <u>heart</u> cycle (SP - DP)

* Normally: 30–40 mm Hg

* Directly proportional to <u>SV</u> and inversely proportional to <u>arterial compliance</u>

* Low/narrow <u>pulse pressure</u> due to ↓ <u>SV</u> (e.g., advanced <u>congestive heart failure</u>, <u>shock</u>, <u>cardiac tamponade</u>, <u>aortic stenosis</u>)

* High/wide <u>pulse pressure</u> due to ↑ <u>SV</u> (e.g., exercise, <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>aortic regurgitation</u>, <u>anemia</u>, <u>obstructive sleep apnea</u>) or stiff <u>arteries</u> (<u>isolated systolic hypertension</u> in elderly)





#### Wall tension




* Definition: the force within vessel walls that counteracts vessel rupture during expansion, thus holding the vascular wall together

* Laplace's law

* Equation: σt = (P<sub>tm</sub> × r) / 2h

* σt = wall tension (mm Hg)

* P<sub>tm</sub> = <u>transmural</u> pressure (mm Hg)

* r = inner radius (cm)

* h = wall thickness (cm)

* Interpretation:

* Increases in wall tension are proportional to increases in pressure across the vessel wall (<u>transmural</u> pressure).

* Wall tension increases with decreasing wall thickness, increasing <u>transmural</u> pressure and/or increasing the inner diameter.

* Given a constant <u>transmural</u> pressure, the smaller the vascular radius and thicker the vascular wall, the less wall tension generated.





> [!NOTE]
> Vessels of the high-pressure system (<u>arteries</u>) have thick vessel walls and smaller internal diameters that enable them to withstand high internal pressures, while vessels of the low-pressure system (<u>veins</u>) have thin vascular walls and larger diameters.




### Blood vessel elasticity



* Definition: the ability of a blood vessel to return to its original shape after expanding




#### Vascular compliance




* Definition: the ability of a vessel to expand in response to changes in pressure

* Equation: C = ΔV/ΔP

* C = compliance (mL/mm Hg)

* ΔV = change in volume (mL)

* ΔP = change in pressure (mm Hg)

* Greater compliance: greater increase in vascular volume during an increase in pressure (e.g., <u>elastic arteries</u>)

* Less compliance: less increase in vascular volume during an increase in pressure (e.g., <u>muscular arteries</u>)





#### Vascular elastance




* Definition: the ability of a vessel to adapt to intraluminal pressure in response to changes in volume (i.e., the reciprocal of compliance)

* Equation: E' = ΔP/ΔV

* E' = elastance (mm Hg/mL)

* C = compliance (mL/mm Hg)

* ΔP = change in pressure (mm Hg)

* ΔV = change in volume (mL)

* Greater elastance: greater change in blood pressure during blood volume change

* Less elastance: less change in blood pressure during blood volume change





> [!NOTE]
> Compliance is mainly determined by the muscle tone of vessel walls. <u>Arterioles</u>, which are abundant in <u>smooth muscle</u>, have low compliance and are, therefore, considered <u>resistance vessels</u>. <u>Veins</u> are less abundant in <u>smooth muscle</u>, have much higher compliance, and are considered <u>capacitance vessels</u>.

## Blood pressure regulation

### <u>Sensors of blood flow regulation</u>




#### Baroreceptors




* Definition: stretch-sensitive nerve endings that detect and regulate blood pressure in <u>systemic circulation</u> via signaling to the <u>autonomic nervous system</u>

* Location: wall of the carotid sinus, <u>aortic arch</u>, <u>atria</u>, and venae cavae

* Mechanism of action: baroreceptor reflex

* <u>Baroreceptors</u> detect ↓ BP → ↓ firing frequency of <u>baroreceptors</u> → ↓ signaling to the <u>brain stem</u> (vasomotor center) → ↓ <u>parasympathetic</u> stimulation and ↑ <u>sympathetic</u> innervation → <u>vasoconstriction</u> → ↑ HR, <u>SV</u>, and BP

* <u>Baroreceptors</u> detect ↑ BP → ↑ firing frequency of <u>baroreceptors</u> → triggering of <u>baroreceptor reflex</u> in <u>brain stem</u> (vasomotor center) → ↑ <u>parasympathetic</u> stimulation and ↓ <u>sympathetic</u> innervation → vasodilatation → ↓ HR, <u>SV</u>, and BP

* Only suitable for making short-term changes in blood pressure (e.g., acute hemorrhage) because their activity (i.e., their firing frequency) adapts to a new blood pressure level within a few days.

* A component of <u>Cushing reflex</u> (<u>hypertension</u>, <u>bradycardia</u>, and respiratory <u>depression</u>): ↑ intracranial pressure → compensatory constriction of cerebral <u>arterioles</u> → ↓ cerebral <u>perfusion</u> → <u>hypercapnia</u> and <u>acidosis</u> → <u>chemoreceptor</u> mediated <u>sympathetic</u> response → ↑ blood pressure → stimulation of <u>aortic arch</u> <u>baroreceptors</u> → activation of the <u>parasympathetic nervous system</u> (vagus) → reflex <u>bradycardia</u>





#### Volume receptors




* Definition: specialized <u>receptors</u> that detect blood flow changes in the <u>pulmonary circulation</u> and regulate blood flow through the <u>autonomic nervous system</u>, <u>atrial natriuretic peptide</u> (<u>ANP</u>), and <u>antidiuretic hormone</u> (<u>ADH</u>)

* Location: <u>pulmonary artery</u> and cardiac <u>atria</u> (low-pressure system)

* Mechanism of action: See <u>atrial reflex</u> and <u>diuresis reflex</u>.





#### Chemoreceptors




* Definition: specialized <u>receptors</u> that detect changes in <u>pH</u> and respiratory gases and regulate <u>pH</u> level, O<sub>2</sub>, and CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations through respiration

* Types

* Peripheral <u>chemoreceptors</u>

* Location: carotid body and aortic body

* Function: measure <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> (< 60 mm Hg), CO<sub>2</sub>, and <u>pH</u>

* Central <u>chemoreceptors</u>

* Location: <u>medulla oblongata</u>

* Function: measure <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u> and <u>pH</u> of the cerebral <u>interstitial</u> fluid

* Central <u>chemoreceptors</u> are less sensitive to PO<sub>2</sub> levels, compared to the peripheral ones.

* Central <u>chemoreceptors</u> become desensitized in response to chronic <u>hypoxia</u> and <u>hypercapnia</u> (e.g., <u>COPD</u>).

* Mechanisms of action

* ↑ CO<sub>2</sub>, ↓ O<sub>2</sub>, and ↓ <u>pH</u> → ↑ <u>sympathetic</u> innervation

* Modulate breathing via the <u>respiratory center</u> in the medulla





> [!NOTE]
> If the <u>baroreceptors</u> of the <u>carotid sinus</u> are too sensitive, even small stimuli, such as turning the head or the pressure of a shirt collar, can lead to excessive blood pressure reduction and even fainting. This is referred to as <u>carotid sinus syndrome</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Carotid massage</u>, which stimulates the <u>baroreceptors</u> in the <u>carotid sinus</u>, is an effective way of reducing the <u>heart rate</u> by increasing the <u>refractory period</u> of the <u>AV node</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Peripheral <u>chemoreceptors</u> are more effective in responding to chronic <u>hypoxia</u> than central <u>chemoreceptors</u>.




### Central <u>blood pressure regulation</u>




* Localization: <u>solitary nucleus</u> in the <u>medulla oblongata</u>

* Receives information (afferents) via:

* The <u>glossopharyngeal nerve</u> (IX): from <u>carotid sinus</u> (vascular dilatation located at carotid <u>artery</u> bifurcation) <u>baroreceptor</u> and carotid body <u>chemoreceptor</u>

* The <u>vagus nerve</u> (X): from aortic <u>chemoreceptor</u>, aortic <u>baroreceptor</u>, and atrial <u>volume receptors</u>

* Sends information (efferents) via:

* <u>Sympathetic</u> cervical chain and <u>sympathetic</u> fibers: to <u>blood vessels</u>, <u>SA node</u>, and <u>AV node</u>

* <u>Parasympathetic</u> <u>vagus nerve</u>: to <u>AV node</u> and <u>SA node</u>





|  | <u>Sympathetic</u> stimulation | <u>Parasympathetic</u> stimulation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Arteries</u> | <br>* Arterial constriction → ↑ <u>peripheral vascular resistance</u><br><br> | <br>* Arterial vasodilatation via the release of <u>nitric oxide</u> (NO) only in <u>coronary arteries</u> and vessels of the <u>penis</u> (<u>erection</u>)<br><br> |
| <u>Veins</u> | <br>* Venous constriction → ↑ <u>preload</u> → ↑ <u>stroke volume</u><br><br> | <br>* Venous dilatation → ↓ <u>preload</u> → ↓ <u>stroke volume</u><br><br> |
| <u>Heart</u> | <br><br>* ↑ Contractility<br><br>* ↑ <u>Heart rate</u><br><br><br> | <br>* ↓ <u>Heart rate</u><br><br> |





![Baroreceptor and chemoreceptor pathways](media/intiujox72y1os10nh89lov6.jpg)

Baroreceptor and chemoreceptor pathways




### <u>Atrial natriuretic peptide</u> (<u>ANP</u>) and <u>antidiuretic hormone</u> (<u>ADH</u>) regulation




#### Atrial reflex




* Definition: a physiologic reflex characterized by an increased <u>heart rate</u> in response to atrial distention (increased <u>venous return</u> to the <u>heart</u>). It is mediated by stretch <u>receptors</u> in the <u>atria</u>.

* Mechanisms of action: ↑ Volume → ↑ atrial stretch <u>receptors</u> stimulation → activation of stretch <u>receptors</u> (<u>B-fibers</u>) in the <u>atria</u> → ↑ <u>sympathetic</u> innervation and no change in <u>parasympathetic</u> innervation → ↑ HR





#### Atrial natriuretic peptide (<u>ANP</u>) secretion pathway




* ↑ Volume → ↑ atrial stretch <u>receptors</u> stimulation→ release of <u>ANP</u> from atrial <u>cardiomyocytes</u> ;  which results in:

* ↑ Excretion of NaCl and water by the <u>kidneys</u> (via <u>afferent arterioles</u> dilations and <u>efferent arterioles</u> constriction)

* ↓ Na<sup>+</sup> reabsorption at the renal collecting tubule (via ↑ <u>cGMP</u>)

* Inhibition of <u>renin</u>

* <u>Vasodilation</u> of <u>veins</u> and <u>arteries</u> (↓ <u>preload</u> and ↓ <u>afterload</u>)

* ↓ Volume → ↓ atrial stretch <u>receptors</u> stimulation → ↓ Release of <u>ANP</u> → ↓ excretion of NaCl and water by the <u>kidneys</u>





#### Diuresis reflex (Gauer-Henry reflex)




* Definition: a physiological reflex that adapts <u>ADH</u> release in the <u>hypothalamus</u> according to blood pressure

* Mechanisms of action

* ↑ BP: Atrial stretch <u>receptors</u> inhibit <u>ADH</u> release via afferent <u>vagal</u> fibers → ↑ water excretion by the <u>kidneys</u>

* ↓ BP: ↑ <u>ADH</u> release → ↓ water excretion by the <u>kidneys</u>





### Renal regulation




* Mechanism of action: release of <u>renin</u> from the juxtaglomerular cells → activation of <u>RAAS</u> → direct <u>vasoconstriction</u> and ↑ extracellular volume (↑ <u>sodium</u> and water reabsorption, ↓ <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>, ↑ <u>pH</u>)

* <u>RAAS</u> is stimulated by:

* <u>Hyponatremia</u>

* Decreased blood <u>osmolality</u>

* Decreased <u>renal blood flow</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>RAAS</u> plays a key role in long-term <u>blood pressure regulation</u> and is, therefore, an ideal target for the treatment of <u>arterial hypertension</u>. While <u>beta blockers</u> decrease <u>renin</u> release by the <u>kidneys</u>, the conversion of <u>angiotensin I</u> to <u>angiotensin II</u> by <u>angiotensin-converting enzyme</u> (<u>ACE</u>) can be influenced by <u>ACE inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>ramipril</u>, <u>enalapril</u>). The effect of <u>angiotensin II</u> on <u>target cell</u> <u>receptors</u> can be inhibited by <u>AT1 receptor</u> <u>antagonists</u> (e.g., <u>candesartan</u>, <u>losartan</u>).

---

## Perfusion

### <u>Perfusion</u>




Definition: the passage of the blood through the <u>circulatory system</u> to the <u>capillary bed</u> to deliver oxygen and <u>nutrients</u> to the tissue and remove waste products (e.g., removal of CO<sub>2</sub> to the <u>lungs</u>)




| <u>Perfusion</u> levels of various organs |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organs | <br>% of <u>cardiac output</u> at rest<br> | % of <u>cardiac output</u> during exercise |
| <br><u>Viscera</u> (hepatic-<u>splanchnic</u> circulation) | 24 | 1 |
| <u>Skeletal muscle</u> | 20 | 88 |
| <u>Kidneys</u> | 19 | 1 |
| <u>Brain</u> | 13 | 3 |
| Other organs | 10 | 1 |
| <u>Skin</u> | 8 | 2 |
| <u>Heart muscle</u> | 3 | 4 |





### Regulation of organ <u>perfusion</u>




Although blood pressure is the primary determinant of <u>perfusion</u>, various other mechanisms maintain constant blood flow within organs.




#### Autoregulation




* Myogenic autoregulation: <u>Myocytes</u> in the walls of <u>arteries</u> and <u>arterioles</u> react to changes in blood pressure to maintain constant blood flow in the <u>blood vessels</u>.

* Mechanism of action: ↑ BP → ↑ <u>transmural</u> pressure in <u>arteries</u> and <u>arterioles</u> (e.g., during strenuous exercise, the transition from <u>supine</u> to upright position) → stretch-activated ion channels opening up in <u>myocytes</u> → <u>myocyte</u> <u>depolarization</u> and subsequent <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> influx → <u>smooth muscle</u> contraction → <u>vasoconstriction</u>

* Sites of action: almost all organs (especially the <u>kidneys</u> and <u>brain</u>) except the <u>lungs</u>

* Local metabolites

* Mechanism of action: the release of vasoactive substances

* Nitric oxide (NO)

* Produced in <u>endothelium</u> by NO-synthase from <u>arginine</u> → <u>vasodilation</u>

* NO production is triggered by:

* Increased BP

* Activation of <u>endothelial</u> <u>receptors</u> by binding of vasoactive substances (e.g., <u>serotonin</u>, <u>bradykinin</u>) → increased release of NO

* Other substances: kinin, <u>histamine</u>, <u>serotonin</u>, <u>prostaglandins</u>, thromboxane

* Sites of action: <u>arteries</u> and <u>arterioles</u>





#### Central regulation




* Mechanisms

* <u>Sympathetic</u> innervation

* <u>Catecholamines</u> from <u>adrenal medulla</u>

* <u>Receptors</u>

* Alpha-1 <u>receptors</u> → <u>vasoconstriction</u>

* Beta-2 <u>receptors</u> → <u>vasodilation</u>

* Differing effects of <u>catecholamines</u>

* <u>Epinephrine</u>: acts on both <u>receptor</u> types but has a greater affinity for <u>beta-2 receptors</u>

* Low concentrations: stronger effect on <u>beta-2 receptors</u> → <u>vasodilation</u>

* High concentrations: stronger effect on <u>alpha-1 receptors</u> → <u>vasoconstriction</u>

* <u>Norepinephrine</u>: mainly acts on <u>alpha-1 receptors</u> → <u>vasoconstriction</u>





#### Autoregulation of specific organs




* <u>Heart</u>

* Local metabolic autoregulation: <u>Adenosine</u> and NO cause <u>vasodilation</u> of the <u>coronary arteries</u> to increase blood flow and <u>oxygen delivery</u> to the <u>myocardium</u>.

* Has the highest arteriovenous O<sub>2</sub> difference of all organs (O<sub>2</sub> extraction at rest ∼ 60–80%)

* During exercise, there is limited capacity to increase <u>myocardial</u> oxygen extraction (small coronary flow reserve).

* <u>Lungs</u>

* Adjustment of vascular <u>perfusion</u> to ventilation

* <u>Hypoventilation</u> (<u>hypoxia</u>) causes <u>vasoconstriction</u> (<u>Euler-Liljestrand mechanism</u>).

* <u>Kidneys</u>

* <u>Myogenic autoregulation</u>

* <u>Tubuloglomerular feedback</u>

* <u>Brain</u> 

* Local metabolic autoregulation (CO<sub>2</sub>, <u>pH</u>) → <u>vasodilation</u>

* <u>Myogenic autoregulation</u>

* <u>Skeletal muscle</u>

* At rest: <u>sympathetic</u> innervation

* During exercise: local metabolic and chemical autoregulation due to an increase in H<sup>+</sup>, <u>lactate</u>, CO<sub>2</sub>, <u>adenosine</u>, and <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>

* Blood flow can be increased (20–30 times) during exercise

* Local metabolic and chemical autoregulation due to an increase in H<sup>+</sup>, <u>lactate</u>, CO<sub>2</sub>, <u>adenosine</u>, and <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>

* Blood flow increases (up to 20–30 fold)

* <u>Skin</u>

* <u>Thermoregulation</u> (via <u>capillaries</u> and arteriovenous <u>anastomoses</u>) determines <u>perfusion</u> levels.

* Mainly <u>sympathetic</u> innervation (<u>vasoconstriction</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>lungs</u> are the only organs in which <u>hypoxia</u> causes <u>vasoconstriction</u>. This is to ensure that <u>perfusion</u> only occurs in areas that are well ventilated. In all other organs, <u>hypoxia</u> leads to <u>vasodilation</u> to improve <u>perfusion</u> and maintain oxygen supply.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Hypoperfusion</u> of vital organs (e.g., <u>hypovolemic shock</u>, <u>cardiogenic shock</u>) is detected by <u>baroreceptors</u> and <u>volume receptors</u>, leading to an increase in <u>sympathetic</u> tone. Autoregulatory mechanisms are then triggered and lead to centralization of blood flow away from the extremities (<u>skeletal muscle</u>, <u>skin</u>), the <u>GI tract</u>, and other internal organs to maintain <u>perfusion</u> of the <u>heart</u> and <u>brain</u>. In addition, <u>vasoconstriction</u> of precapillary <u>resistance vessels</u> raises <u>systemic vascular resistance</u> and reduces <u>hydrostatic pressure</u> in <u>capillaries</u>, increasing the reabsorption of <u>interstitial</u> fluids into vessels.




> [!NOTE]
> To remember the local metabolites used in autoregulation of <u>skeletal muscle</u>, consider to “CAll HuLK”: CO<sub>2</sub>, Adenosine, H<sup>+</sup>, Lactate, <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>.

---

## Capillary fluid exchange

<u>Capillaries</u>, which have the highest total cross-sectional area and lowest flow rate of all <u>blood vessels</u>, are the site of fluid exchange.




### Definitions




* Hydrostatic pressure: the pressure exerted by any fluid on the wall of an enclosed space

* <u>Intravascular</u> <u>hydrostatic pressure</u> 

* The force exerted by the blood confined within blood vessel walls (e.g., <u>capillary</u> <u>hydrostatic pressure</u>)

* Drives fluid out of <u>capillaries</u> and into the <u>interstitium</u>

* Osmotic pressure

* The minimum pressure needed to prevent the flow of a solvent across a semi-permeable membrane

* Determined by concentration gradients: Solvent from a lower concentration solution is drawn across a semi-permeable membrane (via <u>osmosis</u>) into a higher concentration solution.

* Directly proportional to the concentration of solute in the solvent

* Opposes <u>hydrostatic pressure</u>

* Oncotic pressure (<u>colloid osmotic pressure</u>)

* An <u>intravascular</u> <u>osmotic pressure</u> generated by <u>proteins</u> (especially <u>albumin</u>)

* Keeps <u>intravascular</u> fluid within <u>blood vessels</u> and opposes <u>intravascular</u> <u>hydrostatic pressure</u>





### Starling forces




For information on the <u>Starling equation for the glomerulus</u> see <u>measurement of renal function</u> in <u>physiology of the kidney</u>.




* Four <u>Starling forces</u> determine the net flow of fluid between the <u>capillaries</u> and <u>interstitium</u>.

* <u>Capillary</u> <u>hydrostatic pressure</u> (P<sub>c</sub>): drives fluid out of the <u>capillary</u>

* <u>Interstitial</u> <u>hydrostatic pressure</u> (P<sub>i</sub>): attenuates filtration or drives fluid into <u>capillaries</u>

* Plasma <u>colloid (oncotic) pressure</u> (π<sub>c</sub>): drives fluid into the <u>capillary</u>

* <u>Interstitial</u> fluid <u>colloid osmotic pressure</u> (π<sub>i</sub>): drives fluid out of the <u>capillary</u>

* Net fluid flow = J<sub>v</sub> = K<sub>f</sub> [(P<sub>c</sub>- P<sub>i</sub>) - σ(π<sub>c</sub> - π<sub>i</sub>)]

* K<sub>f</sub> = coefficient for vessel permeability to fluid

* σ = Staverman reflection coefficient for vessel permeability to protein

* Net filtration (<u>capillary fluid exchange</u>)

* Depends on the <u>hydrostatic pressure</u> gradient (P<sub>c</sub>- P<sub>i</sub>) and the <u>oncotic pressure</u> gradient (π<sub>c</sub> - π<sub>i</sub>)

* Filtration of fluid out of the <u>capillary</u> usually occurs on the arterial side of the <u>capillary bed</u>, mostly because of pressure from the arterial circulation (increased P<sub>c</sub>) and high plasma fluid levels (decreased π<sub>c</sub>).

* Absorption of fluid into the <u>capillary</u> usually occurs on the venous side of the <u>capillary bed</u>, mostly because of <u>capillary</u> flow resistance (decreased P<sub>c</sub>) and higher relative <u>plasma protein</u> levels following water filtration into the <u>interstitium</u> (increased π<sub>c</sub>).

* Outward filtration volume (arterial side) = inward filtration volume (venous side) + 10%

* 10% of the filtered fluid is returned via <u>lymphatics</u> rather than <u>blood vessels</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Edema</u> is caused by the net movement of fluid into the <u>interstitium</u> if there is an increase in <u>capillary</u> <u>hydrostatic pressure</u> (due to <u>heart failure</u> or Na<sup>+</sup> retention), an increase in <u>interstitial</u> fluid <u>oncotic pressure</u> (due to lymphatic stasis) or a decrease in <u>capillary</u> <u>oncotic pressure</u> (due to <u>cirrhosis</u>, <u>nephrotic syndrome</u>, <u>heart failure</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Burns</u>, infections or toxins can affect vessel permeability (increased K<sub>f</sub>) and can, therefore, result in the formation of <u>edema</u>.
